items.name: Matsue Castle
items.kicker: One of Japan's twelve original castle keeps
items.body:
Built in 1611 and never rebuilt — the black-timbered keep is original, not a postwar concrete replica like most "castles" travelers see in Japan. Climb the narrow original staircases inside for a Lake Shinji view from the top.

Admission {{fact:matsue-castle-tenshu-1200-yen}} (adult, individual rate — prices rose from ¥800 on Jul 1 2026, funding restoration work; a generic guide still quoting the old figure is out of date). Open 8:30–17:00 October–March, last entry 16:30, no closure days.

Busiest roughly 10am–3pm, when tour buses cluster and the donjon staircase gets genuinely congested; arriving right at opening or from ~16:30 is noticeably calmer, per multiple local visitor accounts.

items.name: Izumo Taisha
items.kicker: Japan's oldest shrine, and the only one worshipped with four claps
items.body:
Second only to Ise Jingu in Shinto significance, and architecturally distinct — the honden's soaring roofline and the enormous shimenawa (braided straw rope) over the Kaguraden hall are unlike any other shrine on a typical Japan itinerary.

Grounds open 6:00–19:00, free; the rear precinct — including Soga-no-yashiro behind the main hall — closes at 16:30 for security, so leave the back of the precinct for the early afternoon, not the end of the visit. The Treasure Hall (Shinkoden, a separate building, {{fact:izumo-taisha-treasure-hall-300-yen}} adult) runs 8:30–16:30, last admission 16:00 — the shrine's own site doesn't publish the hall's fee or hours, so this comes from the Izumo tourism association's listing.

Worship here is two bows, four claps, one bow — not the two-clap pattern used almost everywhere else in Japan.

img.file: Izumo-taisha Shrine, Izumo City, Shimane Prefecture, September 2014.jpg
img.alt: Izumo Taisha's torii gate and stone approach

items.name: Iwami Ginzan (Omori & Ryugenji Mabu)
items.kicker: UNESCO World Heritage silver-mining valley, reached by a 6-seat cart
items.body:
Omori was one of the world's largest silver-mining towns in the 16th–17th centuries; the preserved merchant houses along the valley road still have people living in them. The actual mine tunnel, Ryugenji Mabu, sits 2.3 km up-valley and is open for walk-through visits along a ≈400m lit stretch.

Private cars are banned past the park entrance — get there by the no-reservation Ginzan Cart (6 seats, closed Wednesdays) or on foot (≈45 min each way). The operator publishes a daily run COUNT, not an interval — 12–14 runs across 8:00–18:00 — so treat the next cart as up to an hour away rather than half an hour. That is the trip's real physical-feasibility test for a group of 8: two loads minimum, and the second half of the party can lose most of an hour waiting, which is why this sight owns a whole afternoon rather than a slot.

Note the arrival geography: the Iwami Ginzan World Heritage Center, where the bus from Ota-shi runs, is not in the village — the operator puts it about five minutes by road from the Omori townscape, with another bus leg between the two.

items.name: Tanabe Museum of Art
items.kicker: A quiet detour inside Shiomi Nawate — same block as the castle, none of the crowd
items.body:
Tucked inside Shiomi Nawate next to the Lafcadio Hearn Old Residence, entered through an unassuming long-gate — a lower-profile stop than the castle or the main tourist street despite sitting on the same block. The collection is tea-ceremony ware — scrolls, ceramics, lacquer — gathered across 23 generations by the Tanabe family, tatara ironmasters at Yoshida (now Unnan) since the Muromachi period, which is a straighter line into Shimane's own history than the castle gives you. 310-5 Kitahori-cho, Matsue · 0852-26-2211. Worth folding into the Day 1 walk at no extra transit cost.

The museum's own visitor page gives 9:00–17:00, last admission 16:30, closed Mondays (open when a public holiday falls on one); ¥700 adult, ¥500 high-school/university, free below that. The group discount starts at 10 people, so a party of 8 pays the individual rate — don't wait at the desk expecting otherwise.

⚠ Two catches worth a phone call: the museum swaps the permanent display for special exhibitions, which are priced separately and replace the standing collection entirely, and it doesn't publish a 2026 exhibition calendar online. Also note the 16:30 last admission is the same as the castle's — see Day 1 for which one wins on a late arrival.

items.claim: "October is when all of Japan's gods gather at Izumo Taisha" is treated as a calendar fact travelers can time a trip around.
items.correction: The Kamiari-zuki gathering follows the old lunar calendar's 10th month, not October on the Gregorian calendar. In 2026 the actual festival period is Nov 9 – Dec 8 — a trip in late October sees the shrine itself, not the gathering.

items.claim: ICOCA/Suica-type IC cards "work everywhere in Japan, including rural lines."
items.correction: The JR West ICOCA area on the San-in Line ends at Izumo-shi Station. One stop further west — the direction of Odashi and Iwami Ginzan — IC taps stop working entirely; carry cash or buy a paper ticket before crossing that boundary.

items.claim: Older trip reports quote Matsue Castle admission at ¥800.
items.correction: Individual adult admission rose to ¥1,200 on Jul 1 2026, funding tenshu restoration work — a real, recent, and easy-to-miss price jump for anyone reading pre-2026 writeups.

items.claim: Iwami Ginzan and Izumo Taisha are treated as interchangeable day-trip destinations regardless of which weekday you visit.
items.correction: Wednesday is the region's default closure day for small heritage-tourism operators: the Ginzan Cart, the 240-year-old Arakiya soba house at Izumo Taisha, and Gungendo's Omori café are all closed. None of this is obvious from a single venue's own page — it only shows up by checking each one.

items.claim: "Best Matsue food" lists routinely put Kawakyo, a Shinjiko-shichin restaurant, near the top without mentioning capacity.
items.correction: Two independent firsthand accounts confirm Kawakyo seats only at an 8–10 seat counter, typically booked out roughly a month ahead — it can't seat a group of 8 as one party. Matsu-no-Daidokoro Konekkoya's documented 24-seat room is the one that actually fits this trip; Kawakyo is worth the detour if the group ever splits into a smaller subset.
